newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium charges up on LME, ends at six-week peak.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium charges up on LME, ends at six-week peak.

text.p: Aluminium prices broke higher during late Wednesday LME trading, with the clearance of the $1,640 level triggering an influx of fresh speculative buying, traders said.
The market, which was also underpinned by a contraction in the contango and another solid stock fall, closed near six-week highs.
Inventories fell by 6,700 tonnes, the latest in a string of daily drawdowns, although the market did not respond to this until the afternoon when fund buying emerged.
Borrowing of nearby dates kicked in at that time, and by the end of the kerb cash/threes was at $23/25, against $29 contango on Tuesday.
Last three months trade was at $1,661 a tonne, up $29 from Tuesday.
Inventories are expected to continue falling, which should encourage further speculative buying, and the next objective is pegged at $1,700, they said.

Copper also came alive to some extent during the latter part of the session, although the market's advances were not enough to clear the current broad $60 technical range which has a ceiling around $2,380.

Nevertheless, last trade was at the day's peak of $2,370, up $10 from yesterday, with the market also aided by a late widening in the cash/threes spread backwardation to $60/65 and expectations that the run of inventory increases will come to an end soon.
Nickel prices were boosted during the kerb by the late afternoon strength elsewhere in the complex, and raced up to clear the $7,600 level. Last business was at $7,610, up $140 from Tuesday.
A similar move was seen in zinc, which advanced after a previously lackustre session, with last business at $1,287, up $10, and the day's high.
However, tin and lead failed to make an impression, with both metals continuing to languish around midsesison levels.
Tin closed at $5,795, a loss of $5, after meeting resistance around $5,800. Lead was $1 lower at $625.
The alloy market ended at a steadier $1,510/15 a tonne.
